title: Highly Trained Female Runners Show Greater Durability and Physiological Resilience Than Performance-Matched Male Counterparts
authors: Jaen-Carrillo D, Bruce CD, Lawley JS, Zanini M
journal: Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports
population: Highly trained runners matched for performance: 11 female, 11 male
findings: A 180-min treadmill run at standardised moderate intensity with 12-min uphill time trials every 60 min (total 36 +/- 3 km females, 42 +/- 3 km males).
After 3 h, time-trial speed declined less in females than males (-1% vs -10%, p<0.01), with smaller reductions in carbohydrate oxidation and RER.
Females showed greater resilience for maximal isometric knee-extensor force, HR and perceived exertion (p<0.05); peak HR and VO2 were unchanged in both sexes.
Running economy deteriorated similarly between sexes.
limitations: 22 runners, laboratory treadmill, distance not matched between sexes (males ran farther), single protocol; authors say distance-matched conditions need study.
implications: Do not apply a single sex-agnostic durability or decoupling prior: allow a sex term (Smyth 2022 also found larger and earlier decoupling in males) but keep it weak and let athlete data override it.
Fuelling in long runs may need sex-specific attention; this paper gives no fuelling prescription, so no change to nutrition rules is justified.

verification.notes: Crossref and PubMed match (Scand J Med Sci Sports 2026 May;36(5):e70299). Design recorded as cross-sectional (between-sex comparison of matched groups) instead of crossover.
